list.listitem: The diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) can be made based on clinical symptoms, pulmonary function tests (PFTs) or CXR consistent with restrictive lung disease, exclusion of other interstitial lung disease (ILD) and typical findings on high-resolution CT.B

Patients with newly diagnosed ILD and an HRCT scan consistent with probable UIP, indeterminate for UIP, or for an alternative diagnosis should have bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and surgical lung biopsy. B
Consider referral to a tertiary care center specializing in interstitial lung diseases if local multidisciplinary expertise (pulmonology, radiology, pathology) is not available.C
Nintedanib and pirfenidone decrease the decline in FVC and are recommended for use if FVC is between 50% to 80% and patients have a progressive phenotype.B
Nerandomilast shows promise in Phase 3 trials for slowing progression of both idopathic and progressive pulmonary fibrosis. B
Diagnoses of IPF before the use of high-resolution CT and the development of a consensus classification system in 2002 may be suspect. C

background.definition: IPF is one form of ILD characterized by unexplained chronic exertional dyspnea, and presents with cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, and finger clubing. It is rare under the age of 50. Diagnoses prior to 1990 may be inaccurate, as the use of high-resolution CT scan has improved diagnosis. Additionally, classification and terminology had been confusing until consensus definitions were developed in 2002 and updated in 2013 and 2018. Other known causes of ILD should be excluded including environmental and occupational exposures, connective tissue disease, and drug toxicity.

list.listitem: People with IPF have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (acute coronary syndrome elative risk [RR] is 3.14; 95% CI, 2.02-4.87) and deep-vein thrombosis (RR 3.39; 95% CI, 1.57-7.28).
There is an increased risk of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in patients with IPF; in one study 88% had some degree of OSA.

Comorbid conditions include pulmonary hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux, obesity and emphysema. Additionally, patients with IPF are 5x more likely to have a pro-thrombotic clotting defect defined by the presence of at least one marker of fibrinolytic dysfuntion or an acquired or inherited clotting defect. (OR 4.78; 95% CI, 2.93-7.80).

The cause of IPF is unknown. Previously, it was considered an inflammatory reaction to some type of exposure. Current thought is that IPF is a fibrotic process that involves poor wound healing following repeated lung injury. Current research is focused on oxidant, fibrotic, and immunomodulatory processes in the lung in response to repeated injury.

Environmental exposures are associated with IPF: ever smoking, agriculture/farming, livestock, wood dust (pine), metal dust (brass, lead,steel), stone/sand (stone cuttinge/polishing), raising birds, hair dressing and exposure to vegetable and animal dust.
There is increasing study on genetic factors involved in IPF. A familial form acounts for <5% of IPF cases.

The UK Biobank study with over 400,000 participants, demonstrated an association of an unfavorable lifestyle—defined by current smoking, physical inactivity, poor diet, excessive alcohol use, and abnormal body weight—with a more than twofold increased risk of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (HR 2.27). When combined with high genetic risk, the risk rose nearly eightfold (HR 7.80); approximately one-third of cases (32.7%) were attributable to this combined effect.
Suspect IPF in patients with: unexplained chronic exertional dyspnea; cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, and finger clubing; age greater than 50 years; and no better diagnosis. C
CXR and PFTs show findings consistent with restrictive lung disease. A
Typical findings on high-resolution CT show a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern. A

Patients with newly diagnosed ILD who have a HRCT scan consistent with probable UIP, indeterminate for UIP, or an alternative diagnosis, British guidelines (2018) conditionally recommend performing bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and surgical lung biopsy. B

Differential.Differential_Name: Asthma, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), allergic rhinitis
Differential.Differential_Features: Common, cough only and not associated with progressive dyspnea; heartburn seen with GERD; sneezing, itching, nasal discharge with allergic rhinitis

Differential.Differential_Name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), congestive heart failure (CHF)
Differential.Differential_Features: Common; CXR and PFTs distinguish or echocardiogram for CHF
Granulomas on CXR, angiotensin-converting enzyme positive, sarcoid
Female predominance; diagnosis of connective tissue disease by physical examination and lab work
History of exposue (antineoplastic drugs, radiation injury, amiodarone)

list.listitem: Clinical suspicion, exclusion of other ILDs, and presence of a typical IPF pattern on HRCT.

Consider this diagnosis in a person over the age of 50 with unexplained chronic exertional dyspnea who presents with cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, and finger clubing. Other causes of unexplained cough and dyspnea should be considered, with attention to occupational or environmental exposures, drug side effects, unidentified connective tissue disease, and other unidentified infectious, pulmonary or cardiovascular diseases (eg, COPD, CHF).

The only physical examination finding consistently associated with IPF is bibasilar end-inspiratory "Velcro" crackles in 80% of patients. These may not be present very early in the presentation. Clubbing is found in 25% to 50% of patients. In late disease, physical findings of right-sided heart failure and cyanosis may be present.

The sensitivity (62%) and specificity (97%) of clinical diagnosis is based on the absence of history and examination findings suggesting another etiology, slow onset of dyspnea over a 6-month period, and bibasilar end inspiratory "Velcro" crackles. In a study of 39 patients with ILD, academic and community physicians agreed on a diagnosis of IPF in only 33% of cases. In 28% of cases, community physicians diagnosed IPF while academic physicians diagnosed another ILD.

Undifferentiated connective disease can cause lung damage making it difficult to distinguish between ILD of the collagen-vascular form and IPF. Common findings for both are diffuse arthralgias, Raynaud's, and esophageal symptoms. Oral ulcerations, renal or neurologic disease, alopecia, and muscle weakness would be more suggestive of ILD, collagen-vascular form. Nonsmoking women presenting with unexplained cough and progressive dyspnea should be carefully considered for undifferentiated connective disease as the cause of their lung difficulties.
Laboratory tests are used to rule out other causes and should be ordered only as clinically indicated. Baseline lab includes CMP, CBC, and UA.

British guidelines (2018) recommend ordering serological testing to exclude connective tissue disease as a cause of ILD. This should include c-reactive protein, ESR, rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, anti-nuclear antibody titer and pattern. A positive ANA in a low titer (<1:160) or positive rheumatoid factor occur in up to 20% of patients with IPF. Granuloma disease: angiotensin-converting enzyme. Others: EKG, cardiac workup—ECG will be normal in the absence of pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease.

When IPF is suspected, a high-resolution CT scan (HRCT) should be done. The positive predictive value of a HRCT for a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) is 90-100%. HRCT can be classified as UIP which is IPF, possible UIP, and inconsistent with UIP.

On high-resolution CT, patients with UIP have: presence of reticular opacities often associated with traction bronchiectasis; honeycombing, usually 3 to 10 mm cystic airspaces, but up to 2.5 cm, usually subpleural; and absence of features inconsistent with UIP pattern. Reticular opacity scoring may assist with predicting potential for progression.

Patients with newly diagnosed ILD who have a HRCT scan consistent with probable UIP, indeterminate for UIP, or an alternative diagnosis, British guidelines (2018) conditionally recommendat performing bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and surgical lung biopsy.

For patients with newly diagnosed ILD and an HRCT pattern of UIP, British guidelines (2018) strongly recommend against performing surgical lung biopsy, transbronchial lung biopsy, and lung cryobiopsy. They also conditionally recommend against performing BAL.

A variety of biomarkers (serum surfactant protein A and D, matrix metalloprotease, osteopontin) are being studied to assist in diagnosis in patients that can not tolerate biopsy or HRCT. These biomarkers currently have variable ability to identify PF, and potentially to be prognostic for risk of progression or risk of flares. British guidelines (2018) recommend against using serum biomarkers solely for the purpose of distinguishing IPF from other interstitial lung diseases.

A clinical-radiologic-physiologic score can be used to predict probability of survival. Given the poor treatment options currently available, this information can be useful for patient planning and for consideration of lung transplant.

A better score is associated with: younger age, absence of clubbing, no smoking, minimal interstitial opacities on CXR, no evidence of pulmonary hypertension on CXR, and higher predicted total lung capacity (TLC) and PaO2 at the end of maximal exercise.
If IPF is suspected (unexplained chronic exertional dyspnea), order CXR and PFTs.
If criteria are consistent with IPF, order high-resolution CT to confirm diagnosis.
If atypical high-resolution CT findings or atypical clinical features are present (age <50 years, duration <3 months, or absence of restrictive pattern), consider lung biopsy.

Refer patients to a tertiary care center specializing in IPF for diagnosis if multidisciplinary expertise is not available; for enrollment in a clinical trial; or for consideration of lung transplant. C
Nintedanib and pirfenidone are both approved for patients with a interstitial lung disease and may slow progression. B
Corticosteroids, supplementary oxygen, and pulmonary rehabilitation may provide symptomatic relief. C
Immunizations, avoidance of respiratory illnesses, and treatment for GERD make sense. C
Best treatment of acute exacerbations of IPF and co-morbid pulmonary hypertension is unclear. C
Nerandomilast shows promise in Phase 3 trials for slowing progression of both idopathic and progressive pulmonary fibrosis. B

A network meta-analysis of RCTs of drug therapy for IPF identified 48 studies of 22 drug treatments and 10,326 patients. They concluded that nintedanib, pirfenidone, and sildenafil reduce mortality with moderate certainty. They also concluded that sildenabil reduces acute exacerbations and hospitalizations, and that nintedanib, nintedanib plus sildenafil, apirfenidone, and pamrevlumab slow the decline in FVC.

A systematic review of drug therapy identified 30 studies with 16 differ treatments, involving 6865 patients. Decline in FVC >10% was reduced similarily between nintedanib and pirfenidone—nintedanib 0.61 (95% CI, 0.48-0.78) and pirfenidone 0.52 (95% CI, 0.41-0.67). There was a trend toward significance for decrease in respiratory specific death—nintedanib 0.63 (95% CI, 0.36-1.08) and pirfenidone 0.58 (95% CI, 0.33-1.00). Similarily, there was a trend toward significance for decrease in all cause mortality—nintedanib 0.70 (95% CI, 0.45-1.09) and pirfenidone 0.69 (95% CI, 0.45-1.04).

Nintedanib, an antifibrotic that inhibits a variety of tyrosine kinase receptors, also reduced the decline in FVC and was approved in 2020 for patients with progressive disease. Randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trials (INPULSIS1, INPULSIS2) involved 1066 patients using nintedanib 150 mg oral bid for 52 weeks. The mean FVC at enrollment was 80%. The rate in decline in FVC was less in nintedanib groups compared to placebo: INPULSIS1 FVC −114.7 compared to −239.0 for a difference of 125.3 (95% CI, 77.7-172.8; P ≤0.001); INPULSIS2 FVC −113.6 compared to −207.9 for a difference of 93.7 (95% CI, 44.8-142.7; P ≤0.001). Diarrhea was the primary side effect with 5% of the patients in the nintedanib group dropped out due to diarrhea. A pooled analysis of the trials suggested that the benefit may be greater in those with a baseline FVC ≤70% of predicted.

A study randomized 147 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis to an oral preferential phosphodiesterase 4B inhibitor (nerandomilast) 18 mg twice daily or placebo. In patients without previous antifibrotic use, the change in FVC was 5.7 ml with BI 1015550 compared with –81.7 ml in those receiving placebo. In patients who had background antifibrotic use, the FVC increased 2.7 ml with active drug compared with a decrease of 59.2 ml in the placebo group. Both differences were highly significant both clinically and statistically. The drug has received an FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation. A subsequent Phase 3 trial of the drug, now called nerandomilast, with 1176 patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis also showed a slowing in the decline in FVC.

Among 274 patients with IPF and a DlCO of 35% or less of the predicted value who were randomized to nintedanib alone or nintedanib plus sildenafil no significant benefit was seen in the St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) at week 12 or the secondary end points of dyspnea and safety.

Pirfenidone, an antifibrotic, also reduced the decline in FVC. Randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (ASCEND) involved 55 patients using pirfenidone 2403 mg/day for 52 weeks. In the primary analysis, the proportion of patients who had a decline of >10% in FVC or who died was reduced by 47.9% (16.5% in the pirfenidone group compared to 31.8% in the placebo group, p <0.001). Nausea or diarrhea led to treatment discontinuation in 2.2% and rash in 2.9% of the pirfenidone group.

A combined analysis of 3 trials similarly found that that continued treatment with pirfenidone reduced the likelihood of subsequent FVC decline or death. Another study with 1247 patients from two trials found that pirfenidone was associated with a lower likelihood of hospitalization over a one year period (7% vs 12%; p = 0.001).

N-acetylcysteine compared to a control group without usage may improve 6 minute walking distance and slow declines in predicted vital capacity, but does not improve forced vital capacity, rates of adverse events, or death rates.

An RCT of routine antimicrobial therapy involing 513 patients with IPF (254 randomided to either co-trimoxazole or doxycycline) and 259 to usual care failed to demonstrate any benefit with regards to hospitalizations or death.

The ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT guidelines (2015) recommend against the use of the following agents: corticosteroid monotherapy, colchicine, cyclosporin A, combined corticosteroid and immune-modulator therapy, interferon gamma 1b, etanercept, anticoagulation (warfarin), ambrisentan, imatinib and combined acetylcysteine/azathioprine/prednisone. Bosentan and sildenafil have a conditional recommendation against use.
5-year survival rates after lung transplantation in IPF are estimated at 50% to 56%.
Supplemental oxygen and pulmonary rehabilitation can be used for symptom relief as indicated.
Routine monitoring of FVC, DLCO, and six minute walk test (oxygen need) every 3 to 6 months if clinically stable.

The American Thoracic Society (ATS) recommends for patients with ILD: Prescribing home oxygen for at least 15 hours a day (defined as long-term oxygen therapy or LTOT) for patients with ILD and severe hypoxia on room air. Severe hypoxia is defined as having a PaO2 of 55 mm Hg or lower, or oxygen saturation at 88% or lower as measured by pulse oximetry (SpO2). In patients with edema, hematocrit of 55% or greater, or P pulmonale on electrocardiography, the the ATS defined severe hypoxia as PaO2 between 56 and 59 mm Hg or SpO2 at 89%. The use of ambulatory oxygen in patients with ILDD who develop severe exertional hypoxia on room air (SpO2 88% or lower). In patients with chronic lung disease who are mobile outside of the home and require continuous oxygen flow rates of >3 L/min during exertion, the ATS suggests prescribing portable liquid oxygen.

In patients with severe hypoxemia, 24-hour supplemental oxygen was not superior to 15-hour daily use in reducing hospitalizations or death (124.7 vs 124.5 events per 100 person-years), suggesting no added benefit from continuous oxygen therapy.
Corticosteroids may improve cough-related symptoms and relieve symptoms.

A systematic review identified 9 studies for acute exacerbations of interstitial fibrosis. They found improved survival with high dose steroids (> 1 mg/kg) in patients with non-idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (HR .221, 95% CI .10 to .48) as well as reduced recurrence rates (HR .61) but not for patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.11 for survival).

General advice for patients includes smoking cessation to protect residual lung function, daily walking as tolerated, and measures to avoid pulmonary infections (avoid ill children and adults, influenza and pneumonia vaccines). Exercise has been shown to produce immediate improvements in functional exercise capacity, dyspnea and quality of life but there is no evidence of improved survival or long-term benefit.
Treatment of pulmonary hypertension: there is no strong evidence for or against treatment with sildenafil.Bosentan does not improve functional capacity, symptoms, or mortality.
Treatment of GERD: is recommended.
Treatment of acute exacerbation: use of IV corticosteroids up to a gram per day as supportive care, not curative care; cortisporin A and anticoagulation are used without conclusive results.
A small RCT found improvements in health-related quality of life with exercise training.
Consider referral to a tertiary care center specializing in ILD for accurate diagnosis, current treatment options including clinical trials, and consideration for lung transplant.

An acute, often fatal clinical deterioration has been identified with the acute onset of dyspnea (<30 days), cough, fever, flu-like symptoms, worsening hypoxia, and progressive infiltrates not related to CHF or infection. Two year incidence in patients with IPF is estimated at 9.6%, with 78% mortality.
High-dose corticosteroids and cyclosporin A have been tried in exacerbations but without evidence of efficacy.
Anticoagulation therapy over a 3-year period showed some benefit in a nonblinded, nonrandomized study with NNT = 2 for prevention of exacerbations.

PaO2during exertion is a significant predictor of survival. Patients with oxygen saturation less than 90% after 4 minutes of self-paced stepping using a 20-cm high step have a 4-year survival rate of 39%. If no desaturation occurs, the 4-year survival rate is 96%. A

The median survival is 81 months from onset of illness, and 35 months from time of initial visit to the tertiary center. In one study, median survival after ICU admission was 16 days (9-19); 55 (18-284) days from first respiratory admission; and 1.05 (0.34-1.75) years from IPF diagnosis. B
A clinical decision rule can estimate prognosis. B

Disease progression is characterized by: progressive dyspnea; progressive, sustained decreased from baseline in absolute FVC and/or absolute DLCO(corrected for hemoglobin; progression of fibrosis from baseline on HRCT; and acute exacerbation.

In patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, continuous use of hypnotics was associated with increased all-cause mortality across multiple cohorts, highlighting the need to reevaluate their use in this high-risk population.
